newsitem.title: USA: Arkansas vote on combining two bond programs ahead.
newsitem.headline: Arkansas vote on combining two bond programs ahead.

text.p: A bond proposal on Arkansas' November 5 ballot calls for the state's sewer and water bond programs to be combined and would authorize issuance of up to $300 million bonds.

The proposal would limit issuance by the Arkansas Soil and Water Conservation Commission to $60 million per two-year budget period, with higher amounts possible, but subject to General Assembly approval, Ron Hill, bond fund manager for the commission, said.
Arkansas currently runs a Water Resources Development General Obligation Bond Program as well as a Waste Disposal and Pollution Abatement Facilities General Obligation Bond Program, Hill said.
The $300 million limit would not represent a jump in new issuing power, but would merely combine the remaining issuing authority of each program, he said.
Combining the programs would increase administrative efficiency, add flexibity and be more cost effective, Hill said.
The proposal has already been authorized by the legislature and signed by former Governor Jim Guy Tucker, he said.

"In issuing bonds it costs you legal fees and administrative fees for each bond issue," Hill said. "So if we can combine and only have to issue one versus two, we cut the administrative and issuance cost."
The state bond program allows local water and sewer issuers to obtain project funds at a lower rate.
The state channels the borrowing costs as well as any issuance costs on to the borrower. Hopefully, the issuers will pass on the savings to Arkansas' citizens, he said.

Arkansas general obligation debt is double-A rated, and the state can borrow at a much lower rate than local water and sewer districts, most of which are non-rated. Only five cities in Arkansas are rated, Hill said.

As for flexibility, combining the programs would allow needed programs to proceed, regardless of whether they are water or sewer projects. Currently, the state is past is biennium limit for water projects, but has money left on the sewer side.

The legislature authorized the current water program in 1981 and voters approved it in 1982. The program allowed a total of $100 million of bonds, not to exceed $15 million in any two-year budget period.
"We're out of that," Hill said. "We've already issued $15 million this biennium."

Hill said he currently has $8 million to $10 million more of water projects on his books. But on the waste disposal and pollution abatement side, which allows $50 million per two-year budget period and has a $250 million cap, the state has money left over.

"I have not even come close to using that $50 million in any one biennium, because demand has not been there," he said. "So right now, if I had these two programs combined--if it was in effect today--I would take and use more money for water."
Next year may bring more demand on the sewer project side, he said.
